newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Irish airline joins Nordic price war.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Irish airline joins Nordic price war.

text.p: Ireland's cut price airline, Ryanair, on Wednesday joined the price war in Nordic skies that is threatening Scandinavian airline SAS and British Airways' hold over the market.
Ryanair announced it was starting two daily return flights from London's Stansted airport to Stockholm's Skavsta airport from June 12 and pledged to slash fares to Stockholm by over 50 percent.
The move was seen adding to the competitive pressures in the region that has seen SAS and British Airways cut fares in half for limited periods this year.
"Ryanair will break the duopoly of SAS and British Airways on the London-Stockholm route," Ryanair's chief executive Michael O'Leary said in a statement.

The 12-year-old airline, which has a fleet of 17 Boeing 737-200 aircraft, promised more than 70 percent of seats would be available at the two lowest fares of 99 pounds ($157) and 129 pounds -- compared with SAS and British Airways' lowest fares of 220 pounds.
Ryanair does not offer passengers free meals, offers one class of travel, uses secondary, low cost airports, and has a passenger to employee ratio of 4,440 to one against SAS' 904 to one.

"We are the 'low fares, no frills' airline and make no apologises for the fact that we don't give you free newspapers, free meals and drinks," said O'Leary, whose company has said it may list later this year.
"What we do provide is the lowest fares... and an unmatched punctuality record."
Ryanair is the latest airline to challenge SAS, launching services to the "Golden Triangle" that links Oslo, Copenhagen and Stockholm.
SAS had no immediate plans to take defensive action against Ryanair but did not rule out price cuts.
"Of course we will defend our position and if needs be we will lower our prices to do this," SAS spokesman Ulf Ingnas said.

SAS, whose planes flew 63.5 percent full in 1996, is already on its guard after seeing eight airlines starting up operations in its patch. It saw a 31 percent drop in pre-tax profits to 1.82 billion crowns ($237 million at current rates), and predicted tougher competition.

Airline analysts said that while competition is hotting up on European regional market generally, there is particular interest in Stockholm and Copenhagen where the airports have plenty of spare capacity for newcomers.
"But European regional business accounts for about 60 percent of SAS's business so it is more susceptible to competition," one London-based analyst said.
The past year has seen SAS come under pressure from rivals.
Virgin Express now operates two daily flights from its Brussels base to Copenhagen, discounting SAS fares by up to 37 percent, and is known to have grander plans.
But it is not just outsiders eyeing the market. Domestic carriers are also spreading their wings.
Denmark's Maersk Air is now running a Copenhagen-Stockholm flight and servicing the London/Gatwick-Copenhagen route, while Denmark's Sun Air flies to Manchester.
Norway's Braathens SAFE, having bought into Sweden's second largest carrier Transwede, threw down the gauntlet in October 1996 and started flights on the Oslo-Stockholm route.
"The competition is going to get even tougher this year," said one analyst.
